"""Compare semantic data quality across a whole country or operator.

Live (downloads the MobilityData catalogue and fetches each feed), so this is the
one scenario that is not exercised offline:

    python 10_macro_scale_audit.py --country FR --limit 25

Are the data-quality anomalies local bugs, or global architecture choices of an
operator? This filters the world catalogue to a country, audits every reachable
feed with one call, and ranks the classes by how widely they fire — turning the
per-feed audit into a cross-corpus comparison.
"""

import argparse
import collections

import gbfs_toolkit as gb


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--country", default="FR", help="ISO country code to scan")
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=25, help="cap the number of systems")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    # 1. The world inventory, filtered to one country.
    catalog = gb.systems_catalog()
    national = gb.filter_catalog(catalog, country_code=args.country)
    ids = national["system_id"].astype(str).tolist()[: args.limit]
    print(f"{args.country}: {len(national)} systems in the catalogue, auditing {len(ids)}\n")

    # 2. Fetch and audit them all in one call (heuristic-free, declared types).
    verdict, status = gb.audit_catalogue(ids, catalog=catalog, a7_scope="all")
    reachable = sum(1 for s in status.values() if s.startswith("ok"))
    print("Coverage:", dict(collections.Counter(s.split(":")[0] for s in status.values())))
    print(f"Audited {reachable}/{len(ids)} feeds, {len(verdict)} stations\n")

    # 3. How widely does each class fire across the corpus?
    if len(verdict):
        flags = [f"A{i}" for i in range(1, 8)]
        per_system = verdict.groupby("system_id")[flags].max()
        print("Systems flagged per class:")
        print(per_system.sum().to_string())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Collect, store and release data (experimental)
docs.text:
Experimental

These modules were added in 2.1.0. They are public and tested, but their names, parameters and output columns may change in a minor release while they are used on more systems (see the API policy). Import each one by its path: from gbfs_toolkit import quality. Pin gbfs-toolkit>=2.1,<2.2 if you build on them.

For a first walk through the whole chain, see the tutorial; for one task at a time, the recipes. aggregate, quality and store accept a frame, an Arrow table, a DuckDB relation or a path, and read a folder in place.

The audit modules answer is this feed trustworthy? These ones answer what did we collect, how complete is it, and how do we hand it to someone who must be able to trust it? They fit together as a pipeline, and each step also works alone:

flowchart LR
    C[collect<br/>poll feeds] --> S[store<br/>Parquet lake]
    S --> Q[quality<br/>coverage, incidents]
    S --> A[aggregate<br/>15 min, hour, day]
    S --> R[release<br/>frozen folder]
    Q --> R
    R --> V[verify<br/>checksums, fingerprint]
    H[history<br/>metadata versions] -.-> R
    M[stations.match<br/>id continuity] -.-> A
    T[trips<br/>published trips] -.-> A
    P[repro<br/>manifest] --> V
Module What it does Page gbfs_toolkit.collect polls feeds politely (User-Agent, ttl, back-off), writes a fragment per poll and gathers closed days into one file per system and day, keeps missing values missing collect gbfs_toolkit.store a Hive-partitioned Parquet lake (system, year, month), common column names, UTC and local time, DuckDB views store gbfs_toolkit.quality daily coverage and status per system, collection gaps, silent feeds, incident registry, ambiguity indicators quality gbfs_toolkit.aggregate availability by 15 minutes, hour or day, with fixed definitions and a conservation check aggregate gbfs_toolkit.history a dated version of a metadata feed, kept only when its content changes history gbfs_toolkit.stations.match which station of this period is which of the last one stations.match gbfs_toolkit.trips published trip files (Lyft/Motivate, Urban Sharing, Bicycle Transit Systems, Vélomagg) into one schema trips gbfs_toolkit.release freeze a closed period into a folder with coverage, incidents, data package, README and checksums release gbfs_toolkit.repro a content fingerprint and a manifest, verification, samples for CI repro gbfs collect / compact / quality / release / verify the same, from the command line command line

docs.title: A complete example, offline
docs.text:
One system, a day of one-minute snapshots, a hole in the middle: store it, check it, aggregate it, freeze it and verify the result. The data are synthetic, so this runs anywhere.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from gbfs_toolkit.aggregate import aggregate_levels
from gbfs_toolkit.quality import add_quality_indicators, assess
from gbfs_toolkit.release import freeze_release, verify_release
from gbfs_toolkit.store import harmonize, read_lake, write_lake

work = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

# 1. Two days of snapshots for two systems; "lakeside" loses 6 hours on the first day.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
frames = []
for system in ("riverside", "lakeside"):
    minutes = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=2 * 1440, freq="min", tz="UTC")
    if system == "lakeside":
        minutes = minutes[(minutes < "2026-03-01T06:00Z") | (minutes >= "2026-03-01T12:00Z")]
    for station in ("s1", "s2"):
        frames.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "system_id": system, "station_id": station, "fetched_at": minutes,
            "num_bikes_available": rng.integers(0, 12, len(minutes)),
            "num_docks_available": rng.integers(0, 12, len(minutes)),
            "capacity": 20,
        }))
raw = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

# 2. Flag the ambiguous rows, give the columns common names and write the lake.
flagged = add_quality_indicators(raw)
tidy = harmonize(flagged, tz="Europe/Paris")
write_lake(tidy, work / "lake", timezones={"riverside": "Europe/Paris", "lakeside": "Europe/Paris"})

# 3. How complete is it? (The window ends yesterday in real use; here the data end on the 2nd.)
report = assess(read_lake(work / "lake"), time_col="observed_at_utc", end="2026-03-02")
print(report.coverage[["date_utc", "system_id", "completeness_pct", "status"]].to_string(index=False))
print(report.incidents[["incident_id", "cause"]].to_string(index=False))

# 4. Quarter-hour, hourly and daily tables that all describe the same rows.
levels = aggregate_levels(tidy.rename(columns={"observed_at_utc": "fetched_at"}), tz="Europe/Paris")
print({name: int(table["n_obs"].sum()) for name, table in levels.items()})

# 5. Freeze the closed period and verify the folder, as a user of the release would.
info = freeze_release(work / "lake", work / "release", name="demo-2026-03",
                      start="2026-03-01", end="2026-03-02", license="CC0-1.0")
print(info["rows"], verify_release(work / "release", deep=True)["ok"])

docs.title: aggregate: 15 minutes, an hour, a day
docs.text:
Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules (2.1.0). See the overview.

aggregate_availability turns minute-level snapshots into a station-by-bucket table whose columns mean the same thing every time. The definitions are fixed:

Column Definition n_obs rows in the bucket, all of them (nothing is dropped or de-duplicated) n_valid rows with a bike count that are not flagged both_zero_suspect; every other column is computed from these bikes_mean, bikes_min, bikes_max, bikes_first, bikes_last the bike count over the valid rows, first and last in time order docks_mean, docks_min the same for free docks (empty if the operator does not publish them) pct_empty share of valid rows with no bike, in % pct_full share of valid rows where the station is full, in %: no free dock, or, if docks are not published and a capacity column exists, bikes at or above capacity pct_renting share of valid rows where is_renting is true, in % pct_both_zero share of all rows flagged both_zero_suspect, in % (counted here, excluded elsewhere) movement_volume sum of the absolute changes of the bike count between two consecutive valid rows of a station at most max_pair_gap (90 s) apart, in the bucket of the second

movement_volume estimates how many bikes moved. A rental and a return within one poll cancel out and are invisible, and it is not a count of trips.

docs.title: The conservation check
docs.text:
The sum of n_obs over all buckets is the number of input rows, at every frequency. This is the property that makes the three levels describe the same data, and aggregate_levels verifies it for you (check_conservation does it by hand).

Buckets are aligned on UTC. With tz (an IANA zone, or {system_id: zone}), the local wall-clock start of each bucket and its UTC offset are added, so a local-time analysis can group on them without redoing the clock change.

docs.title: Large volumes
docs.text:
Besides a pandas frame, aggregate_availability, aggregate_levels and check_conservation take an Arrow table or dataset, a DuckDB relation, or a path: a lake written by store, a folder of Parquet files (the day files and fragments of collect included), a file or a glob. The source is not loaded whole.

engine= What computes Memory "auto" (default) a pandas frame stays on pandas; any other source goes to DuckDB if the duckdb extra is installed, otherwise to the pandas windows below see below "duckdb" one SQL query over the source (windows, aggregates), spilling to a temporary folder bounded by DuckDB (GBFS_TOOLKIT_DUCKDB_MEMORY_LIMIT=4GB caps it) "pandas" window by window (chunk=, one day by default, rounded up to a multiple of freq so that no bucket is split), carrying each station's last row across a boundary so the movement_volume of a pair that straddles two windows is kept one window

The engines agree: n_obs is conserved by each, counts and integer columns are identical, and the other columns differ by floating-point rounding at most. Tests compare them on random data (including repeated instants, missing counts and windows that cut a pair of rows). Two rows of the same station at the same instant are ordered as the source lists them. The time column of a table, relation or path must be a timestamp.

Measured on a synthetic lake of 42 million rows (1000 stations, one poll a minute, 30 days; a laptop with 16 logical CPUs, DuckDB capped at 6 GB): the three levels take 72 s with DuckDB, and 190 s window by window in pandas with about 2 GB; a pandas frame of just two days of that lake (2.9 million rows) already peaks at 6 GB. benchmarks/lake_volume.py reproduces the measure and benchmarks/README.md has the table.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from gbfs_toolkit.aggregate import aggregate_availability, aggregate_levels, check_conservation

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = pd.date_range("2026-03-28T22:00Z", periods=6 * 60, freq="min")   # spans Paris's clock change
snapshots = pd.DataFrame({
    "system_id": "demo", "station_id": "s1", "fetched_at": t,
    "num_bikes_available": rng.integers(0, 15, len(t)),
    "num_docks_available": rng.integers(0, 15, len(t)),
})

hourly = aggregate_availability(snapshots, "1h", tz="Europe/Paris")
print(hourly[["bucket_start_utc", "bucket_start_local", "utc_offset_min", "n_obs", "bikes_mean"]].head(4))

levels = aggregate_levels(snapshots)                  # 15m, 1h, 1d; each one checked
print({name: int(table["n_obs"].sum()) for name, table in levels.items()})
check_conservation(levels["15m"], snapshots)          # raises if an observation went missing

# The same table from an Arrow table, by windows of two hours (what runs without DuckDB)
import pyarrow as pa

table = pa.Table.from_pandas(snapshots, preserve_index=False)
by_windows = aggregate_availability(table, "1h", tz="Europe/Paris", engine="pandas", chunk="2h")
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(hourly, by_windows, check_exact=False)

docs.title: aggregate
docs.text:
Station availability aggregated to 15 minutes, an hour or a day, with fixed definitions.

Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules added in 2.1.0: names, parameters and output columns may change in a minor release (see the API policy).

Minute-level snapshots are too many to plot or to join; what an analysis usually needs is a station-by-bucket table whose columns mean the same thing every time. aggregate_availability produces one, with these definitions (they will not change silently):

n_obs rows in the bucket, all of them. Nothing is dropped or de-duplicated here, so the sum of n_obs over all buckets is the number of input rows, at every frequency (check_conservation verifies it, and aggregate_levels does it for you); n_valid rows that carry a bike count and are not flagged both_zero_suspect (see gbfs_toolkit.quality): the observations every other column is computed from; bikes_mean, bikes_min, bikes_max, bikes_first, bikes_last the bike count over the valid rows (first and last in time order); docks_mean, docks_min the same for free docks (missing when the operator does not publish them); pct_empty share of valid rows with no bike, in %; pct_full share of valid rows where the station is full, in %: no free dock, or, when docks are not published and a capacity column exists, bikes at or above the capacity; pct_renting share of valid rows where the station is renting, in %; pct_both_zero share of all rows flagged both_zero_suspect, in % (counted here, excluded elsewhere); missing if the frame carries no such column; movement_volume sum of the absolute changes of the bike count between two consecutive valid rows of the same station that are at most max_pair_gap (90 s) apart, attributed to the bucket of the second. It estimates how many bikes moved; a rental and a return inside one poll cancel out and are invisible. It is a volume of movement, not a count of trips.

Buckets are aligned on UTC. With tz, the local wall-clock start of each bucket and the UTC offset are added, so a local-time analysis can group on them without recomputing the clock change.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from gbfs_toolkit.aggregate import aggregate_availability
>>> t = pd.date_range("2026-03-01T08:00Z", periods=30, freq="min")
>>> snaps = pd.DataFrame({
...     "system_id": "demo", "station_id": "s1", "fetched_at": t,
...     "num_bikes_available": range(30), "num_docks_available": range(30, 0, -1)})
>>> agg = aggregate_availability(snaps, "15min")
>>> agg["n_obs"].tolist(), agg["bikes_first"].tolist(), agg["bikes_last"].tolist()
([15, 15], [0, 15], [14, 29])
>>> int(agg["n_obs"].sum()) == len(snaps)
True

def aggregate_availability(
    df: Any,
    freq: str = "15min",
    *,
    tz: str | Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    max_pair_gap: str | pd.Timedelta = "90s",
    time_col: str = "fetched_at",
    engine: str = "auto",
    chunk: str | pd.Timedelta = "1D",
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Aggregate station-status rows to buckets of ``freq`` (see the module for the definitions).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : pandas.DataFrame, pyarrow.Table, duckdb relation, str or Path
        One row per station per poll: ``system_id``, ``station_id``, ``time_col`` and
        ``num_bikes_available``; optionally ``num_docks_available``, ``is_renting``,
        ``capacity`` and ``both_zero_suspect``. Duplicated rows are counted; de-duplicate
        first if your source can repeat a poll. Besides a pandas frame, an Arrow table or
        dataset, a DuckDB relation or a path (a lake written by `gbfs_toolkit.store`, a
        folder of Parquet files, a file or a glob) is read without loading it whole; the time
        column of those must be a timestamp.
    freq : str, default "15min"
        A fixed-width frequency: ``"15min"``, ``"1h"``, ``"1D"`` or any other.
    tz : str or mapping, optional
        An IANA zone, or ``{system_id: zone}``, for the local columns.
    max_pair_gap : str or Timedelta, default "90s"
        Longest time between two rows still counted as consecutive for ``movement_volume``.
    engine : {"auto", "duckdb", "pandas"}, default "auto"
        Who computes. A pandas frame stays on pandas under ``"auto"``; any other source goes
        to DuckDB when the ``duckdb`` extra is installed and is otherwise processed window by
        window in pandas (``chunk`` wide), so the memory used is one window, not the table.
        The engines agree: counts and integer columns are identical and the other columns
        differ by floating-point rounding at most (``n_obs`` is conserved by each). Rows with
        the same station and the same time are ordered as the source lists them.
    chunk : str or Timedelta, default "1D"
        Width of a window of the pandas engine on a table, an Arrow dataset or a path (rounded
        up to a multiple of ``freq``, so that no bucket is split).

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        One row per (system, station, bucket) that has at least one row, sorted; columns as in
        `AGGREGATE_COLUMNS`.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For a calendar frequency (``"1ME"``), an unparseable time, an unknown ``engine`` or,
        for a table, a time column that is not a timestamp.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> t = pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-01T08:00Z", "2026-03-01T08:01Z", "2026-03-01T08:02Z"])
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame({"system_id": "a", "station_id": "s", "fetched_at": t,
    ...                    "num_bikes_available": [5, 3, 4]})
    >>> row = aggregate_availability(df, "1h").iloc[0]
    >>> int(row["n_obs"]), float(row["bikes_mean"]), int(row["movement_volume"])
    (3, 4.0, 3)
    """
    table = open_table(df, what="aggregate_availability")
    need_columns(
        pd.DataFrame(columns=table.columns()),
        [*_REQUIRED[:2], time_col, _REQUIRED[2]],
        what="aggregate_availability",
    )
    step = fixed_timedelta(freq, what="freq")
    gap = fixed_timedelta(max_pair_gap, what="max_pair_gap")
    window = fixed_timedelta(chunk, what="chunk")
    use = resolve_engine(engine, table, what="aggregate_availability")
    if use == "duckdb":
        out = _duckdb_aggregate(table, step, gap, time_col)
    elif table.kind == "pandas":
        out = _bucketed(table.df, step, gap, time_col, None)[0]  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    else:
        out = _chunked_aggregate(table, step, gap, time_col, window)
    out = _finish(out, tz)
    _log.info("aggregate: %d rows -> %d buckets of %s (%s)", table.count(), len(out), freq, use)
    return out

docs.text:
check_conservation(aggregated: DataFrame, source: Any) -> None

Raise GBFSValidationError unless the buckets hold exactly the source rows.

The sum of n_obs must equal the number of rows of source (a frame, an Arrow table, a relation or a path): an aggregate that lost or invented an observation is wrong whatever its means look like.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> check_conservation(pd.DataFrame({"n_obs": [15, 15]}), pd.DataFrame({"x": range(30)}))
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/aggregate.py 
def check_conservation(aggregated: pd.DataFrame, source: Any) -> None:
    """Raise ``GBFSValidationError`` unless the buckets hold exactly the source rows.

    The sum of ``n_obs`` must equal the number of rows of ``source`` (a frame, an Arrow
    table, a relation or a path): an aggregate that lost or invented an observation is wrong
    whatever its means look like.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> check_conservation(pd.DataFrame({"n_obs": [15, 15]}), pd.DataFrame({"x": range(30)}))
    """
    got, want = (
        int(aggregated["n_obs"].sum()),
        open_table(source, what="check_conservation").count(),
    )
    if got != want:
        raise GBFSValidationError(
            f"aggregation does not conserve observations: sum of n_obs is {got}, source has {want} rows"
        )

docs.text:
aggregate_levels(df: Any, *, levels: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, verify: bool = True, **options: object) -> dict[str, DataFrame]

The 15-minute, hourly and daily aggregates in one call, each checked for conservation.

Returns {"15m": ..., "1h": ..., "1d": ...} (or the levels you give, name -> freq); options go to aggregate_availability (engine, tz, chunk...). With verify (the default) each level must conserve the observations, so the three tables describe the same rows.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> t = pd.date_range("2026-03-01T00:00Z", periods=200, freq="min")
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"system_id": "a", "station_id": "s", "fetched_at": t,
...                    "num_bikes_available": 3})
>>> out = aggregate_levels(df)
>>> {k: int(v["n_obs"].sum()) for k, v in out.items()}
{'15m': 200, '1h': 200, '1d': 200}
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/aggregate.py 
def aggregate_levels(
    df: Any,
    *,
    levels: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    verify: bool = True,
    **options: object,
) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]:
    """The 15-minute, hourly and daily aggregates in one call, each checked for conservation.

    Returns ``{"15m": ..., "1h": ..., "1d": ...}`` (or the ``levels`` you give, name -> freq);
    ``options`` go to `aggregate_availability` (``engine``, ``tz``, ``chunk``...). With
    ``verify`` (the default) each level must conserve the observations, so the three tables
    describe the same rows.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> t = pd.date_range("2026-03-01T00:00Z", periods=200, freq="min")
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame({"system_id": "a", "station_id": "s", "fetched_at": t,
    ...                    "num_bikes_available": 3})
    >>> out = aggregate_levels(df)
    >>> {k: int(v["n_obs"].sum()) for k, v in out.items()}
    {'15m': 200, '1h': 200, '1d': 200}
    """
    source = open_table(df, what="aggregate_levels")
    result = {}
    for name, freq in (levels or LEVELS).items():
        agg = aggregate_availability(source, freq, **options)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        if verify:
            check_conservation(agg, source)
        result[name] = agg
    return result

docs.title: Command line: collect, compact, quality, release, verify
docs.text:
Experimental

The commands below were added in 2.1.0 and may change in a minor release. gbfs audit is stable. See the overview.

Needs the extras of the library calls behind them: pip install "gbfs-toolkit[fetch,parquet]" (and [cli] for coloured audit tables). Exit codes: 0 success, 1 a check failed (a failed poll, a mismatching release), 2 bad arguments, missing input or a refusal.

docs.title: gbfs collect
docs.text:
Polls feeds politely and writes one fragment per poll under OUT/<feed>/<system>/_fragments/<day>/ (collect); --compact gathers the fragments of closed days into OUT/<feed>/<system>/<day>.parquet when it is done, and --write day rewrites the day file at each poll instead. With none of --interval, --duration and --iterations it polls once.

gbfs collect --system harbor=https://example.org/gbfs/gbfs.json \
             --out data/collected \
             --user-agent "my-lab-gbfs/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)"

# a poll a minute for an hour, vehicles too, and the dated metadata
gbfs collect --systems-file systems.csv --out data/collected \
             --user-agent "my-lab-gbfs/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)" \
             --feeds station_status vehicle_status --metadata \
             --interval 60 --duration 3600

--systems-file is a CSV (system_id plus auto_discovery_url, gbfs_url or url; the output of gbfs_toolkit.systems_catalog works) or a JSON object {system_id: url}. --user-agent is required. --min-interval (seconds, default 1) and the feed's ttl are never undercut; --no-ttl ignores the ttl and you then own the load.

docs.title: gbfs compact
docs.text:
Gathers the fragments of closed days into one file per system and day, atomically and idempotently (running it again changes nothing). Today's fragments (UTC) are left alone unless --include-today.

gbfs compact data/collected                    # both feeds
gbfs compact data/collected --kind station_status --systems harbor

docs.title: gbfs quality
docs.text:
Daily coverage and incidents of a collection (quality). PATH is a collect folder or a lake, read in place (not loaded whole) unless --systems is given.

gbfs quality data/collected --end 2026-03-31 --incidents known-incidents.json --out reports/march
gbfs quality data/lake --layout lake --expected-polls 96 --poll-resolution 15min --strict

It prints, per system, the days in each status and the mean completeness, then the incident counts; --json prints the same as JSON, --out DIR writes daily_coverage.csv and incidents.json, and --strict exits 1 if any system-day is not ok. Leave today out with --end (it is still being collected).

docs.title: gbfs release
docs.text:
Freezes a closed period of a lake into a new folder (release). It uploads nothing and has no default licence.

gbfs release data/lake releases/demo-2026-03 --name demo-2026-03 \
             --start 2026-03-01 --end 2026-03-31 --license CC-BY-4.0 --systems harbor lakeside

docs.title: gbfs verify
docs.text:
Checks a release folder against its SHA256SUMS, or a data manifest against data (repro).

gbfs verify releases/demo-2026-03            # every file matches, none unlisted
gbfs verify releases/demo-2026-03 --deep     # and the content fingerprint matches
gbfs verify data_manifest.json --data data/lake/

docs.title: collect: a polite collector
docs.text:
Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules (2.1.0). See the overview.

gbfs_toolkit.collect.Collector polls the station (and vehicle) feeds of some systems and writes what they publish. You call it; it never starts anything by itself.

docs.title: What it does and refuses to do
docs.text:
It identifies itself user_agent is required, with no default. Give one that tells an operator whom to write to: "my-lab-gbfs/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)". It respects ttl A GBFS document says how long it stays fresh. The collector will not ask again before that, nor before min_interval (1 s by default). respect_ttl=False exists for tests and for a feed whose ttl you know to be wrong; you then own the load you put on it. It backs off A feed that fails is left alone for 2, 4, 8 ... seconds (capped by max_backoff); HTTP retries of 429 and 5xx honour Retry-After. After five failures in a row the feed's URL is looked up again. It uses conditional requests ETag and Last-Modified are sent back; a 304 is not stored again. It never invents a value A field the feed leaves out is stored empty and typed: Int64 counts, boolean flags, float64 coordinates. Never 0, never True. It writes atomically, and never rewrites Each poll of a system is one small fragment file, written to a temporary name and renamed; nothing already written is touched. compact_collected gathers the fragments of each closed day into one file per system and day. One bad feed does not stop the rest A failure is logged and reported in the result table, never raised.

A difference with to_canonical_station_status

The older gbfs_toolkit.to_canonical_station_status turns a missing is_renting into True (and to_canonical_vehicles a missing is_disabled into False): convenient for a one-off look, wrong for a collection, where a station that publishes nothing must not look open. collect keeps the gap. If you have data from an older collector that wrote those defaults, declare it as an ambiguous_missing_value incident in quality.

docs.title: Layout and compaction
docs.text:
<out_dir>/station_status/<system_id>/_fragments/2026-03-01/<time>-<id>.parquet   # one per poll
<out_dir>/station_status/<system_id>/2026-03-01.parquet                          # after compaction
<out_dir>/vehicle_status/<system_id>/...
<out_dir>/metadata/<system_id>/<feed>/<day>.parquet      # with poll_metadata, see history

A day file rewritten whole at each poll costs more as the day grows (fine for a few hundred stations every minute, not for a large system), so a poll only adds a fragment. compact_collected(out_dir) (also Collector.compact(), gbfs compact and gbfs collect --compact) turns the fragments of every closed UTC day into the day file:

  • atomic: the day file is written to a temporary name and renamed, and only then are the fragments that were read removed, so an interruption loses nothing (at worst a fragment is read twice, and the rows that are identical in every column are kept once);
  • idempotent: with nothing to gather it changes nothing and rewrites nothing; running it twice, or two at once, gives the same day file;
  • safe next to a running collector: a fragment written meanwhile is not read, so it is not removed, and it joins the next compaction. Today's fragments (UTC) are left alone unless include_today=True;
  • a fragment that cannot be read is left in place, with a warning.

read_collected, and a path given to aggregate or quality, read day files and fragments alike, so compaction is a matter of file count, not of correctness. Pass write="day" to Collector for the previous behaviour. To go further, load the day files into a lake: write_lake("data/collected/station_status", "data/lake") streams them in, a day at a time.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The getter below stands in for the network, which is how the tests of the module work too; leave get_json out to use HTTP (needs pip install "gbfs-toolkit[fetch,parquet]").

import tempfile

from gbfs_toolkit.collect import Collector, read_collected

docs = {
    "https://example.org/gbfs.json": {"version": "2.3", "data": {"en": {"feeds": [
        {"name": "station_status", "url": "https://example.org/status.json"},
        {"name": "free_bike_status", "url": "https://example.org/bikes.json"}]}}},
    "https://example.org/status.json": {"ttl": 60, "data": {"stations": [
        {"station_id": "7", "num_bikes_available": 4, "num_docks_available": 8, "is_renting": True},
        {"station_id": "8"}]}},                       # a station that publishes nothing
    "https://example.org/bikes.json": {"ttl": 0, "data": {"bikes": [
        {"bike_id": "b1", "lat": 43.61, "lon": 3.87}]}},
}

out = tempfile.mkdtemp()
collector = Collector(
    {"demo": "https://example.org/gbfs.json"}, out,
    user_agent="docs-example/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)",
    feeds=("station_status", "vehicle_status"),
    get_json=docs.__getitem__,          # offline; omit to use HTTP
    min_interval=0,
)
print(collector.poll_once()[["feed", "outcome", "rows"]])
print(collector.poll_once()[["feed", "outcome"]])    # the 60 s ttl: station_status is skipped

stations = read_collected(out)
print(stations[["station_id", "num_bikes_available", "is_renting"]])   # station 8: empty, not 0

# Gather the fragments of closed days into day files (today's are left alone by default)
from gbfs_toolkit.collect import compact_collected

print(compact_collected(out).empty)                         # today is still being collected
done = compact_collected(out, include_today=True)           # here we compact it anyway
print(done[["system_id", "day", "fragments", "rows"]])
assert compact_collected(out, include_today=True).empty     # idempotent: nothing left to do
assert len(read_collected(out)) == len(stations)            # and nothing lost

A bounded loop in your own process (Ctrl-C ends it cleanly):

# not run in the tests (it would take an hour)
collector.run(interval=60, duration=3600)        # one hour, a poll a minute

The same from the shell: see the command line.

docs.title: collect
docs.text:
A polite collector of GBFS station and vehicle snapshots, written one file per day.

Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules added in 2.1.0: names, parameters and output columns may change in a minor release (see the API policy).

Nothing here runs in the background: you call Collector.poll_once, or Collector.run (a loop in your own process, bounded by a duration or a number of iterations), or the gbfs collect command. What it does, and refuses to do:

  • It identifies itself. A user_agent is required (there is no default): give one that tells the operator whom to write to, for example "my-lab-gbfs/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)".
  • It respects the feed's ttl. A GBFS document says how long it stays fresh; the collector will not ask again before that, nor before min_interval. A feed that answers with an error is left alone for longer each time (exponential back-off, capped), and HTTP retries honour Retry-After.
  • It never invents a value. A field the feed leaves out is stored empty, typed (Int64 for counts, boolean for flags, float64 for coordinates), never 0 nor True. A station that publishes nothing must not look like an empty or an open station. (This is stricter than gbfs_toolkit.to_canonical_station_status, which defaults a missing is_renting to True.)

  • It writes atomically, and never rewrites what it has already written. Each poll of a system is one small fragment file, written to a temporary name and renamed::

    /station_status//_fragments/2026-03-01/-.parquet

    compact_collected gathers the fragments of each closed day into one file per system and UTC day, atomically and idempotently (running it again changes nothing, and an interruption loses nothing)::

      <out_dir>/station_status/<system_id>/2026-03-01.parquet
  <out_dir>/vehicle_status/<system_id>/2026-03-01.parquet

    read_collected reads day files and fragments alike, and so does a path given to gbfs_toolkit.aggregate or gbfs_toolkit.quality. write="day" restores the earlier behaviour (the day file is rewritten as a whole at each poll: simple, and fine for a few hundred stations at a one-minute cadence, but its cost grows with the day).

    Networking needs the fetch extra and Parquet the parquet extra. For offline work, pass get_json (a url -> dict function): the tests of this module use a local server.

    Examples:

    >>> import tempfile
>>> from gbfs_toolkit.collect import Collector, read_collected
>>> docs = {
...     "https://example.org/gbfs.json": {"version": "2.3", "data": {"en": {"feeds": [
...         {"name": "station_status", "url": "https://example.org/status.json"}]}}},
...     "https://example.org/status.json": {"ttl": 0, "data": {"stations": [
...         {"station_id": "7", "num_bikes_available": 4, "is_renting": 1},
...         {"station_id": "8"}]}},
... }
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as out:
...     c = Collector({"demo": "https://example.org/gbfs.json"}, out,
...                   user_agent="docs-example/1.0", get_json=docs.__getitem__, min_interval=0)
...     outcome = c.poll_once()
...     snaps = read_collected(out)
>>> outcome["outcome"].tolist(), snaps["num_bikes_available"].isna().tolist()
(['collected'], [False, True])

def __init__(
    self,
    systems: Mapping[str, str] | pd.DataFrame,
    out_dir: str | Path,
    *,
    user_agent: str,
    feeds: Sequence[str] = ("station_status",),
    timeout: float = 15.0,
    retries: int = 2,
    backoff_factor: float = 0.5,
    min_interval: float = 1.0,
    respect_ttl: bool = True,
    max_backoff: float = 3600.0,
    max_workers: int = 4,
    write: str = "fragments",
    get_json: Callable[[str], dict[str, Any]] | None = None,
    session: Any = None,
    clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic,
    now: Callable[[], pd.Timestamp] | None = None,
) -> None:
    if not isinstance(user_agent, str) or not user_agent.strip():
        raise ValueError(
            "user_agent is required: tell the operators who is polling them, "
            "e.g. 'my-lab-gbfs/1.0 (mailto:me@example.org)'"
        )
    if write not in WRITE_MODES:
        raise ValueError(f"write must be one of {WRITE_MODES}, got {write!r}")
    bad = [f for f in feeds if f not in FEED_KINDS]
    if bad or not feeds:
        raise ValueError(f"feeds must be a non-empty subset of {FEED_KINDS}, got {list(feeds)}")
    self.systems = _systems_mapping(systems)
    if not self.systems:
        raise ValueError("no system to collect from")
    if not any(ch in user_agent for ch in ("@", "http")):
        _log.warning(
            "user_agent %r has no contact (e-mail or URL); operators prefer one", user_agent
        )
    self.out_dir = Path(out_dir)
    self.write = write
    self.user_agent = user_agent.strip()
    self.feeds = tuple(dict.fromkeys(feeds))
    self.timeout = float(timeout)
    self.min_interval = float(min_interval)
    self.respect_ttl = respect_ttl
    self.max_backoff = float(max_backoff)
    self.max_workers = max(1, int(max_workers))
    self._get_json = get_json
    self._retries, self._backoff_factor = int(retries), float(backoff_factor)
    self._session = session
    self._clock = clock
    self._now = now or (lambda: pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC"))
    self._state: dict[tuple[str, str], _State] = {}
    self._locks: dict[Path, threading.Lock] = {}
    self._lock = threading.Lock()

Gather the fragments of this collector's feeds into day files (compact_collected).

Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/collect.py 
def compact(
    self,
    *,
    include_today: bool = False,
    now: Callable[[], pd.Timestamp] | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Gather the fragments of this collector's feeds into day files (`compact_collected`)."""
    parts = [
        compact_collected(
            self.out_dir,
            kind,
            systems=list(self.systems),
            include_today=include_today,
            now=now or self._now,
        )
        for kind in self.feeds
    ]
    return pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

def poll_once(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Poll every system and feed once (those still fresh or backing off are skipped).

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        One row per (system, feed): ``system_id, feed, outcome`` (one of `OUTCOMES`),
        ``rows`` written and ``error`` (text, for ``failed``). A failure never raises: it is
        logged and reported here, so one bad feed does not stop the others.
    """
    tasks = [(s, k) for s in self.systems for k in self.feeds]

    def work(task: tuple[str, str]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        try:
            return self._poll_one(*task)
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 (keep the other systems going)
            _log.exception("[%s] unexpected error on %s", *task)
            return {
                "system_id": task[0],
                "feed": task[1],
                "outcome": "failed",
                "rows": 0,
                "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
            }

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=min(self.max_workers, len(tasks))) as pool:
        rows = list(pool.map(work, tasks))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["system_id", "feed", "outcome", "rows", "error"])

Each feed of each system is normalised (to_canonical_*), stamped with fetched_at and handed to gbfs_toolkit.history.record_version, which stores it under <out_dir>/metadata/<system_id>/<feed>/<UTC day>.parquet only if it differs from the latest version. def poll_metadata(self, feeds: Sequence[str] = METADATA_FEEDS) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fetch the slowly changing feeds and keep a version only when their content changed.

    Each feed of each system is normalised (``to_canonical_*``), stamped with ``fetched_at``
    and handed to `gbfs_toolkit.history.record_version`, which stores it under
    ``<out_dir>/metadata/<system_id>/<feed>/<UTC day>.parquet`` only if it differs from the
    latest version. Call it once a day; it does not wait for a ``ttl``.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        ``system_id, feed, outcome`` (``written``, ``unchanged``, ``unavailable``, ``failed``
        or a `gbfs_toolkit.history.VersionResult` action) and ``error``.
    """
    from gbfs_toolkit.history import record_version
    from gbfs_toolkit.io import normalize as nz
    from gbfs_toolkit.io.fetch import parse_discovery

    bad = [f for f in feeds if f not in METADATA_FEEDS]
    if bad:
        raise ValueError(
            f"unknown metadata feed(s) {bad}; expected a subset of {METADATA_FEEDS}"
        )

    def normalise(feed: str, doc: dict[str, Any], system: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        if feed == "system_information":
            return pd.DataFrame([nz.to_canonical_system_information(doc, system_id=system)])
        if feed == "station_information":
            return nz.to_canonical_station_info(doc, system_id=system)
        if feed == "vehicle_types":
            return nz.to_canonical_vehicle_types(doc, system_id=system)
        if feed == "system_pricing_plans":
            return nz.to_canonical_pricing_plans(doc, system_id=system)
        return nz.to_canonical_system_regions(doc, system_id=system)

    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for system, url in self.systems.items():
        try:
            urls, _ = parse_discovery(self._fetch(url).data)
        except GBFSError as exc:
            _log.warning("[%s] discovery failed: %s", system, exc)
            rows += [
                {"system_id": system, "feed": f, "outcome": "failed", "error": str(exc)}
                for f in feeds
            ]
            continue
        for feed in feeds:
            row = {"system_id": system, "feed": feed, "outcome": "unavailable", "error": None}
            rows.append(row)
            if feed not in urls:
                continue
            try:
                frame = normalise(feed, self._fetch(urls[feed]).data, system)
                frame = frame.assign(fetched_at=self._now())
                folder = self.out_dir / "metadata" / system / feed
                row["outcome"] = record_version(frame, folder).action
            except (GBFSError, ValueError, TypeError, KeyError) as exc:
                _log.warning("[%s] %s failed: %s", system, feed, exc)
                row.update(outcome="failed", error=str(exc))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["system_id", "feed", "outcome", "error"])

def run(
    self,
    *,
    interval: float = 60.0,
    duration: float | None = None,
    max_iterations: int | None = None,
    sleep: Callable[[float], None] = time.sleep,
    on_poll: Callable[[int, pd.DataFrame], None] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Poll every ``interval`` seconds for ``duration`` seconds or ``max_iterations`` polls.

    With neither bound it runs until you interrupt it (Ctrl-C ends it cleanly). The loop
    lives in your process; nothing is left running when it returns.

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        ``iterations``, ``rows`` written and ``outcomes`` (a count per outcome).
    """
    if interval <= 0:
        raise ValueError("interval must be positive")
    started = self._clock()
    outcomes: Counter[str] = Counter()
    rows = 0
    iteration = 0
    try:
        while True:
            t0 = self._clock()
            iteration += 1
            result = self.poll_once()
            outcomes.update(result["outcome"])
            rows += int(result["rows"].sum())
            if on_poll is not None:
                on_poll(iteration, result)
            if max_iterations is not None and iteration >= max_iterations:
                break
            pause = max(0.0, interval - (self._clock() - t0))
            if duration is not None and self._clock() - started + pause >= duration:
                break  # the next poll would fall after the end
            sleep(pause)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        _log.info("interrupted after %d iteration(s)", iteration)
    return {"iterations": iteration, "rows": rows, "outcomes": dict(outcomes)}

A station_status document as one row per station, missing values left missing.

Reads the GBFS 2 and 3 field names (num_vehicles_available and vehicle_docks_available stand in for the 2.x names). Counts are Int64, flags boolean, last_reported and fetched_at tz-aware UTC.

Examples:

>>> doc = {"data": {"stations": [{"station_id": "a", "num_bikes_available": 2},
...                              {"station_id": "b", "is_renting": False}]}}
>>> out = parse_station_status(doc, system_id="demo")
>>> out["is_renting"].tolist()[0] is pd.NA, out["is_renting"].tolist()[1]
(True, False)
>>> out["num_bikes_available"].isna().tolist()
[False, True]
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/collect.py 
def parse_station_status(
    doc: Mapping[str, Any], *, system_id: str, fetched_at: pd.Timestamp | None = None
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """A ``station_status`` document as one row per station, missing values left missing.

    Reads the GBFS 2 and 3 field names (``num_vehicles_available`` and
    ``vehicle_docks_available`` stand in for the 2.x names). Counts are ``Int64``, flags
    ``boolean``, ``last_reported`` and ``fetched_at`` tz-aware UTC.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> doc = {"data": {"stations": [{"station_id": "a", "num_bikes_available": 2},
    ...                              {"station_id": "b", "is_renting": False}]}}
    >>> out = parse_station_status(doc, system_id="demo")
    >>> out["is_renting"].tolist()[0] is pd.NA, out["is_renting"].tolist()[1]
    (True, False)
    >>> out["num_bikes_available"].isna().tolist()
    [False, True]
    """
    when = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC") if fetched_at is None else to_utc([fetched_at]).iloc[0]
    rows = []
    for s in _records(doc.get("data", doc), "stations"):
        bikes = s.get("num_bikes_available")
        docks = s.get("num_docks_available")
        rows.append(
            {
                "system_id": system_id,
                "station_id": _text(s.get("station_id")),
                "fetched_at": when,
                "last_reported": parse_gbfs_timestamp(s.get("last_reported")),
                "num_bikes_available": _int(
                    bikes if not _missing(bikes) else s.get("num_vehicles_available")
                ),
                "num_docks_available": _int(
                    docks if not _missing(docks) else s.get("vehicle_docks_available")
                ),
                "is_renting": _flag(s.get("is_renting")),
                "is_returning": _flag(s.get("is_returning")),
                "is_installed": _flag(s.get("is_installed")),
            }
        )
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=_STATION_COLUMNS)
    for c in ("num_bikes_available", "num_docks_available"):
        df[c] = df[c].astype("Int64")
    for c in ("is_renting", "is_returning", "is_installed"):
        df[c] = df[c].astype("boolean")
    for c in ("system_id", "station_id"):
        df[c] = df[c].astype("string")
    df["fetched_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["fetched_at"], utc=True)
    df["last_reported"] = pd.to_datetime(df["last_reported"], utc=True)
    return df

def parse_vehicle_status(
    doc: Mapping[str, Any], *, system_id: str, fetched_at: pd.Timestamp | None = None
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """A ``free_bike_status`` / ``vehicle_status`` document, one row per vehicle.

    ``vehicle_id`` is read from ``vehicle_id`` or ``bike_id``; a record with neither is skipped.
    Flags that the feed omits stay missing (a vehicle that does not say it is disabled is not
    declared working).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> doc = {"data": {"bikes": [{"bike_id": "b1", "lat": 43.6, "lon": 3.87},
    ...                           {"vehicle_id": "b2", "is_disabled": True}]}}
    >>> out = parse_vehicle_status(doc, system_id="demo")
    >>> out["vehicle_id"].tolist(), out["is_disabled"].isna().tolist()
    (['b1', 'b2'], [True, False])
    """
    when = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC") if fetched_at is None else to_utc([fetched_at]).iloc[0]
    rows = []
    for v in _records(doc.get("data", doc), "vehicles", "bikes"):
        vid = v.get("vehicle_id", v.get("bike_id"))
        if _missing(vid):
            continue
        rows.append(
            {
                "system_id": system_id,
                "vehicle_id": str(vid),
                "fetched_at": when,
                "station_id": _text(v.get("station_id")),
                "vehicle_type_id": _text(v.get("vehicle_type_id")),
                "lat": _float(v.get("lat")),
                "lon": _float(v.get("lon")),
                "is_disabled": _flag(v.get("is_disabled")),
                "is_reserved": _flag(v.get("is_reserved")),
            }
        )
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=_VEHICLE_COLUMNS)
    for c in ("is_disabled", "is_reserved"):
        df[c] = df[c].astype("boolean")
    for c in ("system_id", "vehicle_id", "station_id", "vehicle_type_id"):
        df[c] = df[c].astype("string")
    df["lat"] = df["lat"].astype("float64")
    df["lon"] = df["lon"].astype("float64")
    df["fetched_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["fetched_at"], utc=True)
    return df

read_collected(out_dir: str | Path, kind: str = 'station_status', *, systems: Iterable[str] | None = None, start: str | Timestamp | None = None, end: str | Timestamp | None = None, on_error: str = 'skip') -> DataFrame

Read what a Collector wrote (day files and fragments), for some systems and days.

start and end are UTC days (both inclusive, compared with the file names). An unreadable file (a truncated write, a copy cut short) is skipped with a warning (on_error="skip") or raised (on_error="raise"). The result is sorted by time. If a day has both a day file and fragments (a compaction that was interrupted), rows that are identical in every column are counted once.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> read_collected("/nonexistent/folder").empty
True
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/collect.py 
def read_collected(
    out_dir: str | Path,
    kind: str = "station_status",
    *,
    systems: Iterable[str] | None = None,
    start: str | pd.Timestamp | None = None,
    end: str | pd.Timestamp | None = None,
    on_error: str = "skip",
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read what a `Collector` wrote (day files and fragments), for some systems and days.

    ``start`` and ``end`` are UTC days (both inclusive, compared with the file names). An
    unreadable file (a truncated write, a copy cut short) is skipped with a warning
    (``on_error="skip"``) or raised (``on_error="raise"``). The result is sorted by time. If a
    day has both a day file and fragments (a compaction that was interrupted), rows that are
    identical in every column are counted once.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> read_collected("/nonexistent/folder").empty
    True
    """
    if kind not in FEED_KINDS:
        raise ValueError(f"kind must be one of {FEED_KINDS}, got {kind!r}")
    if on_error not in ("skip", "raise"):
        raise ValueError("on_error must be 'skip' or 'raise'")
    base = Path(out_dir) / kind
    lo = None if start is None else to_utc([start]).iloc[0].strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    hi = None if end is None else to_utc([end]).iloc[0].strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    wanted = None if systems is None else {str(s) for s in systems}
    frames = []
    if base.is_dir():
        require_pyarrow("read_collected")
        for folder in sorted(p for p in base.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
            if wanted is not None and folder.name not in wanted:
                continue
            for day, (whole, pieces) in _day_files(folder).items():
                if (lo and day < lo) or (hi and day > hi):
                    continue
                day_frames = []
                for f in [*whole, *pieces]:
                    try:
                        day_frames.append(pd.read_parquet(f).astype(_DTYPES[kind], errors="ignore"))
                    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 (pyarrow raises several types)
                        if on_error == "raise":
                            raise
                        _log.warning("skipping unreadable file %s: %s", f, exc)
                if whole and pieces and len(day_frames) > 1:  # an interrupted compaction
                    day_frames = [pd.concat(day_frames, ignore_index=True).drop_duplicates()]
                frames.extend(day_frames)
    if not frames:
        return pd.DataFrame(
            columns=_STATION_COLUMNS if kind == "station_status" else _VEHICLE_COLUMNS
        )
    out = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
    sort = ["fetched_at", "system_id", "station_id" if kind == "station_status" else "vehicle_id"]
    return out.sort_values(sort).reset_index(drop=True)

docs.text:
compact_collected(out_dir: str | Path, kind: str = 'station_status', *, systems: Iterable[str] | None = None, include_today: bool = False, now: Callable[[], Timestamp] | None = None, compression: str = 'zstd') -> DataFrame

Gather the fragments of each closed UTC day into one file per system and day.

For every (system, day) that has fragments, the existing day file (if any) and the fragments are combined, rows identical in every column are kept once, the rows are sorted by time and station (or vehicle), and <day>.parquet is written atomically; only then are the fragments that were read removed. The result is therefore safe against an interruption (at worst a fragment is read twice, and its rows are deduplicated by the next compaction), idempotent (nothing left to gather: nothing changes and no file is rewritten), and safe next to a running Collector (a fragment written meanwhile is not read, so it is not removed; it joins the next compaction). A fragment that cannot be read is left in place with a warning. Two compactions at once give the same day file.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default out_dir str or Path

The folder a Collector writes to.

required kind ('station_status', 'vehicle_status') "station_status" systems iterable of str

Only these systems.

None include_today bool

Today's (UTC) fragments are left alone by default: that day is still being collected.

False now callable

A UTC clock, for tests.

None

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

One row per compacted (system, day): kind, system_id, day, fragments, rows, path; empty when there is nothing to do.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> compact_collected("/nonexistent/folder").empty
True
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/collect.py 
def compact_collected(
    out_dir: str | Path,
    kind: str = "station_status",
    *,
    systems: Iterable[str] | None = None,
    include_today: bool = False,
    now: Callable[[], pd.Timestamp] | None = None,
    compression: str = "zstd",
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Gather the fragments of each closed UTC day into one file per system and day.

    For every (system, day) that has fragments, the existing day file (if any) and the fragments
    are combined, rows identical in every column are kept once, the rows are sorted by time and
    station (or vehicle), and ``<day>.parquet`` is written atomically; only then are the
    fragments that were read removed. The result is therefore safe against an interruption (at
    worst a fragment is read twice, and its rows are deduplicated by the next compaction),
    **idempotent** (nothing left to gather: nothing changes and no file is rewritten), and safe
    next to a running `Collector` (a fragment written meanwhile is not read, so it is not
    removed; it joins the next compaction). A fragment that cannot be read is left in place
    with a warning. Two compactions at once give the same day file.

    Parameters
    ----------
    out_dir : str or Path
        The folder a `Collector` writes to.
    kind : {"station_status", "vehicle_status"}
    systems : iterable of str, optional
        Only these systems.
    include_today : bool, default False
        Today's (UTC) fragments are left alone by default: that day is still being collected.
    now : callable, optional
        A UTC clock, for tests.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        One row per compacted (system, day): ``kind, system_id, day, fragments, rows, path``;
        empty when there is nothing to do.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> compact_collected("/nonexistent/folder").empty
    True
    """
    require_pyarrow("compact_collected")
    import pyarrow as pa
    import pyarrow.parquet as pq

    from gbfs_toolkit.store import _drop_duplicate_rows

    if kind not in FEED_KINDS:
        raise ValueError(f"kind must be one of {FEED_KINDS}, got {kind!r}")
    today = (now or (lambda: pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")))().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    wanted = None if systems is None else {str(s) for s in systems}
    id_col = "station_id" if kind == "station_status" else "vehicle_id"
    base = Path(out_dir) / kind
    rows_out: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    if not base.is_dir():
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=["kind", "system_id", "day", "fragments", "rows", "path"])
    for folder in sorted(p for p in base.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
        if wanted is not None and folder.name not in wanted:
            continue
        frag_root = folder / _FRAGMENTS
        if not frag_root.is_dir():
            continue
        for day_dir in sorted(p for p in frag_root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
            day = day_dir.name
            fragments = sorted(day_dir.glob("*.parquet"))
            if not fragments or (day >= today and not include_today):
                continue
            target = folder / f"{day}.parquet"
            tables, read = [], []
            for f in fragments:
                try:
                    tables.append(pq.ParquetFile(f).read())
                    read.append(f)
                except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 (pyarrow raises several types)
                    _log.warning("compaction leaves unreadable fragment %s: %s", f, exc)
            if not tables:
                continue
            if target.exists():
                tables.insert(0, pq.ParquetFile(target).read())
            combined = _drop_duplicate_rows(pa.concat_tables(tables, promote_options="default"))
            order = [("fetched_at", "ascending")]
            if id_col in combined.column_names:
                order.append((id_col, "ascending"))
            combined = combined.sort_by(order)

            def write(tmp: Path, table: Any = combined) -> None:
                pq.write_table(table, tmp, compression=compression)

            atomic_write(target, write)
            for f in read:
                f.unlink(missing_ok=True)
            try:
                day_dir.rmdir()
                frag_root.rmdir()
            except OSError:
                pass  # fragments that arrived meanwhile, or unreadable ones: leave them
            rows_out.append(
                {
                    "kind": kind,
                    "system_id": folder.name,
                    "day": day,
                    "fragments": len(read),
                    "rows": int(combined.num_rows),
                    "path": str(target.relative_to(Path(out_dir))),
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows_out, columns=["kind", "system_id", "day", "fragments", "rows", "path"])

docs.title: history: versions only when the content changes
docs.text:
Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules (2.1.0). See the overview.

system_information, vehicle_types, system_pricing_plans, system_regions and station_information change a few times a year, yet a collector fetches them every day. Overwriting them loses the past; keeping every fetch repeats the same rows hundreds of times. record_version keeps one file per distinct content, named after the UTC day of the fetch:

metadata/harbor/vehicle_types/2026-01-14.parquet      the content as of 14 January
metadata/harbor/vehicle_types/2026-06-02.parquet      it changed on 2 June

Two fetches have the same content when their rows are equal ignoring the fetch time, the order of rows and of columns, the order of keys inside a JSON text, 1 against 1.0, and a column that is absent against one that is empty. The order inside a JSON array does matter.

Result action Meaning written a new version, or the refreshed version of the current UTC day unchanged same content as the latest version: nothing written kept_closed_day a different version of a closed day exists; a closed day is never rewritten older_than_latest the fetch predates the latest version; nothing done

read_version(dir, "latest") returns the newest; read_version(dir, day, asof=True) returns the version in force on a past day, which is what an analysis of a past period needs. Collector.poll_metadata() (collect) does the fetching and the recording for you.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import tempfile
import datetime as dt

import pandas as pd

from gbfs_toolkit.history import content_fingerprint, list_versions, read_version, record_version

def fetch(name, when):
    return pd.DataFrame({"vehicle_type_id": ["bike", "ebike"], "name": [name, "E-bike"],
                         "rules": ['{"a": 1, "b": 2}', "[1, 2]"], "fetched_at": pd.Timestamp(when)})

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
today = dt.date(2026, 7, 1)
print(record_version(fetch("City bike", "2026-01-14T10:00Z"), folder, today=today).action)   # written
print(record_version(fetch("City bike", "2026-02-20T10:00Z"), folder, today=today).action)   # unchanged
print(record_version(fetch("Vélo", "2026-06-02T10:00Z"), folder, today=today).action)        # written

print(list_versions(folder)[["version_date"]])
print(read_version(folder, "2026-03-01", asof=True)["name"].tolist())         # the January version

a = fetch("x", "2026-01-01T00:00Z")
b = a.iloc[::-1].assign(rules=["[1, 2]", '{"b": 2, "a": 1}'], fetched_at=pd.Timestamp("2027-01-01T00:00Z"))
assert content_fingerprint(a) == content_fingerprint(b)    # order and key order do not count

docs.title: history
docs.text:
Keep a dated version of a metadata feed only when its content changes.

Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules added in 2.1.0: names, parameters and output columns may change in a minor release (see the API policy).

system_information, vehicle_types, system_pricing_plans, system_regions and station_information change a few times a year, but a collector fetches them every day. Overwriting them loses the past; keeping each fetch repeats the same bytes hundreds of times. record_version keeps one file per distinct content, named after the UTC day of the fetch::

<history_dir>/2026-01-14.parquet     the content as of 14 January
<history_dir>/2026-06-02.parquet     it changed on 2 June

Two fetches have the same content when their rows are equal ignoring

  • the fetch time (fetched_at changes at every call, see ignore),
  • the order of the rows,
  • the order of the columns,
  • the order of the keys inside a JSON text or a dict ('{"a":1,"b":2}' equals '{"b":2,"a":1}'),
  • 1 against 1.0, and a column that is absent against a column that is empty.

content_fingerprint is that comparison, as a SHA-256 you can store. The list order inside a JSON array does matter. A version of a closed day is never rewritten; the version of the current UTC day may be, so a second fetch the same day replaces the first.

Parquet needs pip install gbfs-toolkit[parquet]; the fingerprint alone needs nothing.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from gbfs_toolkit.history import content_fingerprint
>>> a = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["x", "y"], "rules": ['{"p": 1, "q": 2}', "[]"],
...                   "fetched_at": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01T00:00Z"] * 2)})
>>> b = a.iloc[::-1].assign(rules=['[]', '{"q": 2, "p": 1}'],
...                         fetched_at=pd.to_datetime(["2026-02-01T00:00Z"] * 2))
>>> content_fingerprint(a) == content_fingerprint(b)
True

VersionResult(action: str, version_date: date, path: Path, fingerprint: str)

What record_version decided.

action is "written" (a new or refreshed version), "unchanged" (same content as the latest version), "kept_closed_day" (a different version of a closed day already exists and is never rewritten) or "older_than_latest" (the fetch predates the latest version; nothing is done).

SHA-256 (hex) of a frame's content, as defined in the module description.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default df DataFrame

A metadata table (or any small table).

required ignore sequence of str

Columns left out of the comparison.

``("fetched_at",)``

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> one = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
>>> content_fingerprint(one) == content_fingerprint(pd.DataFrame({"a": [2.0, 1.0]}))
True
>>> content_fingerprint(one) == content_fingerprint(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]}))

Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/history.py 
def content_fingerprint(
    df: pd.DataFrame, *, ignore: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = VOLATILE_COLUMNS
) -> str:
    """SHA-256 (hex) of a frame's content, as defined in the module description.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : pandas.DataFrame
        A metadata table (or any small table).
    ignore : sequence of str, default ``("fetched_at",)``
        Columns left out of the comparison.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> one = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
    >>> content_fingerprint(one) == content_fingerprint(pd.DataFrame({"a": [2.0, 1.0]}))
    True
    >>> content_fingerprint(one) == content_fingerprint(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 3]}))
    False
    """
    skip = set(ignore)
    lines = []
    for record in df.to_dict(orient="records"):
        row = {}
        for key, value in record.items():
            if key in skip or (not isinstance(value, (list, dict)) and _is_na(value)):
                continue
            canon = _canonical(value)
            if canon is not None:
                row[str(key)] = canon
        lines.append(json.dumps(row, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False, default=str))
    lines.sort()
    return hashlib.sha256("\n".join(lines).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

def list_versions(history_dir: str | Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The dated versions present: ``version_date`` (a ``date``) and ``path``, oldest first.

    Files whose name is not ``YYYY-MM-DD.parquet`` are ignored.
    """
    rows = []
    folder = Path(history_dir)
    if folder.is_dir():
        for f in sorted(folder.glob("*.parquet")):
            try:
                rows.append({"version_date": dt.date.fromisoformat(f.stem), "path": f})
            except ValueError:
                continue
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["version_date", "path"])

Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/history.py 
def read_version(
    history_dir: str | Path, version: str | dt.date = "latest", *, asof: bool = False
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a version: ``"latest"``, or the one of a given day.

    With ``asof=True`` a date selects the version that was in force on that day (the latest one
    dated on or before it), which is what an analysis of a past period wants.

    Raises
    ------
    FileNotFoundError
        If no version matches.
    """
    require_pyarrow("read_version")
    versions = list_versions(history_dir)
    if versions.empty:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"no dated version in {history_dir}")
    if isinstance(version, str) and version == "latest":
        row = versions.iloc[-1]
    else:
        day = version if isinstance(version, dt.date) else dt.date.fromisoformat(str(version))
        if asof:
            before = versions[versions["version_date"] <= day]
            if before.empty:
                raise FileNotFoundError(f"no version of {history_dir} on or before {day}")
            row = before.iloc[-1]
        else:
            hit = versions[versions["version_date"] == day]
            if hit.empty:
                raise FileNotFoundError(f"no version of {history_dir} dated {day}")
            row = hit.iloc[0]
    return pd.read_parquet(row["path"])

docs.text:
record_version(df: DataFrame, history_dir: str | Path, *, time_col: str = 'fetched_at', ignore: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = VOLATILE_COLUMNS, dry_run: bool = False, today: date | None = None) -> VersionResult

Save df as a dated version of history_dir unless its content did not change.

The version is dated by the UTC day of the latest time_col in df. With dry_run nothing is written, and the result says what would have been. today overrides the clock (tests).

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If df has no usable time to date the version.

Examples:

>>> import tempfile, pandas as pd
>>> a = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Demo"], "fetched_at": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-05T10:00Z"])})
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
...     first = record_version(a, d, today=pd.Timestamp("2026-02-01").date())
...     again = record_version(a.assign(fetched_at=pd.Timestamp("2026-01-06T10:00Z")), d,
...                            today=pd.Timestamp("2026-02-01").date())
>>> first.action, again.action
('written', 'unchanged')
Source code in src/gbfs_toolkit/history.py 
def record_version(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    history_dir: str | Path,
    *,
    time_col: str = "fetched_at",
    ignore: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = VOLATILE_COLUMNS,
    dry_run: bool = False,
    today: dt.date | None = None,
) -> VersionResult:
    """Save ``df`` as a dated version of ``history_dir`` unless its content did not change.

    The version is dated by the UTC day of the latest ``time_col`` in ``df``. With ``dry_run``
    nothing is written, and the result says what would have been. ``today`` overrides the clock
    (tests).

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``df`` has no usable time to date the version.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import tempfile, pandas as pd
    >>> a = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Demo"], "fetched_at": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-05T10:00Z"])})
    >>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    ...     first = record_version(a, d, today=pd.Timestamp("2026-02-01").date())
    ...     again = record_version(a.assign(fetched_at=pd.Timestamp("2026-01-06T10:00Z")), d,
    ...                            today=pd.Timestamp("2026-02-01").date())
    >>> first.action, again.action
    ('written', 'unchanged')
    """
    need_columns(df, [time_col], what="record_version")
    times = to_utc(df[time_col], what=time_col).dropna()
    if times.empty:
        raise ValueError(f"record_version: {time_col} holds no usable time to date the version")
    day = times.max().date()
    folder = Path(history_dir)
    target = folder / f"{day.isoformat()}.parquet"
    fingerprint = content_fingerprint(df, ignore=ignore)
    current = today or dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc).date()
    versions = list_versions(folder)
    if not versions.empty:
        latest = versions.iloc[-1]
        if content_fingerprint(pd.read_parquet(latest["path"]), ignore=ignore) == fingerprint:
            return VersionResult("unchanged", latest["version_date"], latest["path"], fingerprint)
        if target.exists() and day < current:
            _log.info("version of the closed day %s already exists; kept", day)
            return VersionResult("kept_closed_day", day, target, fingerprint)
        if latest["version_date"] > day:
            _log.info("fetch of %s is older than the latest version; nothing done", day)
            return VersionResult("older_than_latest", day, latest["path"], fingerprint)
    if not dry_run:
        require_pyarrow("record_version")
        atomic_write(target, lambda tmp: df.to_parquet(tmp, index=False, compression="zstd"))
        _log.info("new version of %s: %s", folder, target.name)
    return VersionResult("written", day, target, fingerprint)

docs.title: quality: coverage, gaps and incidents
docs.text:
Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules (2.1.0). See the overview.

A collection is as useful as what you know about its holes. gbfs_toolkit.quality tells you, per system and UTC day, how many of the expected polls arrived and why the others did not.

docs.title: Statuses
docs.text:
Status Meaning ok at least ok_threshold_pct (95 % by default, settable) of the expected polls arrived partial some arrived, not enough, and nothing explains it outage_collector the day overlaps a gap in the collection itself (no poll from any system for an hour or more) or an incident you declared outage_operator the collection was running, yet nothing came from this system

A poll is a distinct slot (one minute by default; poll_resolution="15min" for a slower cadence). A day still being collected counts as partial: pass end= yesterday to leave it out.

docs.title: Indicators that flag and never remove
docs.text:
add_quality_indicators adds three columns to station-status rows. No row is dropped and there is no cleaning pipeline: what to do with a flagged row is your analysis's decision.

Column Meaning field_unsupported_by_operator the operator publishes 0 for a field for the whole month (docks of a dockless system, say): the field is named, and its column is blanked (mask_unsupported=False keeps it) both_zero_suspect zero bikes and zero free docks at a station of positive capacity: more often a placeholder than a state. Missing when a count or the capacity is unknown network_all_zero_anomaly in this poll more than 95 % of the system's rows are at zero on every field it publishes

docs.title: The incident registry
docs.text: An incident has an incident_id, start_utc, end_utc (empty: ongoing), a scope (all or system identifiers separated by commas), a cause and a summary. The causes are outage_collector, outage_operator, unreadable_file and ambiguous_missing_value (a period in which a value and its absence cannot be told apart). You declare what you know; detect_incidents adds the collection gaps and silent feeds it finds, with stable identifiers.

docs.title: Large volumes
docs.text:
daily_coverage, find_collector_gaps, field_unsupported_by_operator, detect_incidents and assess take, besides a pandas frame, an Arrow table or dataset, a DuckDB relation or a path (a lake, a folder of Parquet files, a file or a glob), and an engine= ("auto", "duckdb", "pandas") with the rules of aggregate. What they need from the rows is additive (polls per system, day and slot; distinct minutes; non-empty and zero values per system and period), so DuckDB, or batches of pandas, give the same tables as the frame does. add_quality_indicators returns a row per input row and stays on pandas frames.

QualityReport (what assess returns) reads like the pair of tables it holds: report.coverage and report.incidents, report["coverage"], report.to_frames(), report.to_frame() (the coverage). The columns and logical types of the tables are COVERAGE_COLUMNS / COVERAGE_DTYPES and INCIDENT_COLUMNS / INCIDENT_DTYPES.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from gbfs_toolkit.quality import (
    add_incident, add_quality_indicators, assess, read_incidents, write_incidents)

def poll(system, start, minutes, bikes=3, docks=5):
    t = pd.date_range(start, periods=minutes, freq="min", tz="UTC")
    return pd.DataFrame({"system_id": system, "station_id": "s1", "fetched_at": t,
                         "num_bikes_available": bikes, "num_docks_available": docks, "capacity": 10})

snapshots = pd.concat([
    poll("alpha", "2026-03-01", 3 * 1440),               # complete for three days
    poll("beta", "2026-03-01", 1440),                    # beta goes silent after the first day
    poll("gamma", "2026-03-01", 600), poll("gamma", "2026-03-01T16:00", 480 + 2 * 1440),  # 6-hour hole
])
snapshots = snapshots[~((snapshots.system_id != "gamma")
                        & (snapshots.fetched_at.between("2026-03-01T10:00Z", "2026-03-01T15:59Z")))]

known = add_incident(None, "migration", "2026-02-01", "2026-02-03",
                     cause="ambiguous_missing_value", summary="Older collector wrote 0 for a missing count.")
report = assess(snapshots, known_incidents=known, end="2026-03-03")
print(report.coverage.pivot(index="date_utc", columns="system_id", values="status"))
print(report.incidents[["incident_id", "scope", "cause"]].to_string(index=False))
print(report.summary()["days_by_status"])

write_incidents(report.incidents, "incidents.json")      # .csv works too
assert len(read_incidents("incidents.json")) == len(report.incidents)

flagged = add_quality_indicators(poll("delta", "2026-03-01", 4, bikes=[0, 0, 4, 2], docks=[0, 0, 3, 3]))
print(flagged[["num_bikes_available", "both_zero_suspect"]])

docs.title: quality
docs.text:
Coverage, collection gaps, silent feeds and an incident registry for GBFS snapshots.

Experimental

Part of the experimental data-lake modules added in 2.1.0: names, parameters and output columns may change in a minor release (see the API policy).

A collection of snapshots is only as useful as what you know about its holes. This module answers, for each system and each UTC day, how many of the expected polls arrived, and labels the day:

ok at least ok_threshold_pct (95 % by default) of the expected polls arrived; partial some arrived, not enough, and nothing explains it; outage_collector the day overlaps a gap of the collection itself (no poll from any system for an hour or more) or an incident you declared; outage_operator the collection was running, yet nothing came from this system.

It also flags values that are ambiguous at the source, with three row-level indicators (add_quality_indicators) that flag and never remove: nothing here drops a row, and there is no cleaning pipeline; what to do with a flagged row is the analysis's decision.

field_unsupported_by_operator an operator that publishes 0 for every station for the whole period does not publish the field; the column is blanked and the field named; both_zero_suspect a station of positive capacity reporting no bike and no free dock, more often a placeholder than a real state; network_all_zero_anomaly a poll in which (almost) every station of a system reports zero.

Incidents are kept in a small registry (INCIDENT_COLUMNS) that you can read, write and extend, and that detect_incidents completes with the gaps and silent feeds it finds.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from gbfs_toolkit.quality import daily_coverage
>>> times = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=1440, freq="min", tz="UTC")
>>> snaps = pd.DataFrame({"system_id": "demo", "station_id": "s1", "fetched_at": times})
>>> cov = daily_coverage(snaps)
>>> row = cov.iloc[0]
>>> row["date_utc"].isoformat(), int(row["actual_polls"]), row["status"]
('2026-03-01', 1440, 'ok')
